titleFa: کتاب The Master Algorithm: How the Quest for the Ultimate Learning Machine Will Remake Our World
titleEn: The Master Algorithm: How the Quest for the Ultimate Learning Machine Will Remake Our World
author: Pedro Domingos
introFa: کتاب «The Master Algorithm: How the Quest for the Ultimate Learning Machine Will Remake Our World» نوشته Pedro Domingos یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Master Algorithm: How the Quest for the Ultimate Learning Machine Will Remake Our World»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: INTERVIEW Pedro Domingos on The Master Algorithm: A Conversation with Vasant Dhar Vasant Dhar1 and Pedro Domingos2 Big Data (Vasant Dhar, BIG): Pedro, hats off to you for writing a most excellent book [The Master Algo- rithm: How the Quest for the Ultimate Learning Machine Will Remake Our World]. Well done. There are some fundamental questions I have, beginning with why did you write this book? Did you write it for experts or the general public? Dr. Domingos: I had two main goals. The ﬁrst one was to give a basic understanding, and awareness, of ma- chine learning (ML) to people outside the ﬁeld. Machine learning today is too important to be left to the experts—every citizen, professional, scientist, busi- ness person, and public ofﬁcial needs to know what it is and what it does, because it affects their life and their decisions. (And I’ve seen too many needlessly bad de- cisions made because of a lack of basic understanding of machine learning.) The other goal was to help nudge the ﬁeld in the right direction. I think there is a tendency, in machine learn- ing as in any other ﬁeld, for people to get stuck within particular paradigms and lose sight of the bigger picture. For all its successes, machine learning is still in its infan- cy; we need great new ideas and major breakthroughs if we’re ever going to reach the level of human learning. And paradoxically, people coming into the ﬁeld anew may be in a better position to come up with those ideas than professional researchers who are already working along very speciﬁc tracks. So my hope in writ- ing the book is that it will entice new people, whether students or people in other ﬁelds, into machine learning, and they’ll enrich the ﬁeld with their ideas. BIG: Let’s take this a little further to clarify for differ- ent readers what they should expect to get from read- ing the book. I realize that books are sometimes written at several levels, where the more you know, the deeper your analysis of the material, but where even novices can get a lot out of it. There were sections of the book where I thought, ‘‘Oh, that’s a nice way to talk about trees’’ or ‘‘I never got all the fuss about the role of autoencoders in deep learning.’’ Similarly, I understood better ‘‘why all the fuss about MCMC?’’ But I can’t imagine appreciating these nuggets with- out knowing a fair amount about tree induction or neural nets or Markov decision processes. So, it seems a worthwhile read for people in the ﬁeld. Which is great for many readers of Big Data who have a reasonable degree of knowledge about machine learning and want to connect the dots, but what do you think it would take for a not AI-savvy reader to get something signiﬁcant from your book? Do you suggest that they follow the readings you suggest? Dr. Domingos: I had several different sets of readers in mind when writing the book, each with different needs. One is just the general reader, who has heard a lot about machine learning and is curious—What is the hubbub all about? What is machine learning really? What can and can’t it do? What’s hype and what’s not? What’s the intellectual content of the ﬁeld? What are the implications? How does it affect my life? Another group is businesspeople, managers, inves- tors, policymakers, etcetera, who need to make deci- sions that involve machine learning. They don’t care about the technical details, but they need to know what the key issues, opportunities, and pitfalls are, and to be able to talk to data scientists and critically evaluate what they say. Finally, there are readers who have a professional interest in machine learning. They could already be data scientists, want to become data scientists, or want to start using data science in their jobs. They could be students or researchers. 1Stern School of Business, New York University, New York, New York. 2Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington. And they could be scientists, engineers, or businesspeo- ple who work with data scientists. These readers all have different levels of background, and as a result, the book needs to work on different lev- els as well. I tried to do this by having each chapter or section start with just the key ideas described in ways that anyone can understand, and with plenty of moti- vation. Then there’s usually a part that goes deeper into the algorithms, and that the more general reader can safely skip without losing the thread of the book, as I suggest in the prologue. For readers with a profes- sional interest in machine learning, my book is just a starting point, and a way to get a perspective on the ﬁeld that they wouldn’t get from a textbook. The ‘‘fur- ther readings’’ section at the end of the book gives them pointers for further study, both general (online courses, textbooks, etc.) and speciﬁc to each topic covered. For researchers, my goal is indeed to get them to look be- yond the conﬁnes of the speciﬁc paradigm they work in, see new connections, perhaps have new ideas, whether they step toward the Master Algorithm or any- thing else. BIG: My second question has to do with the issue of the ‘‘art’’ of data science and the role of formulation in crafting good solutions. I deﬁned data science as the study of the generalizable extraction of knowl- edge from data, but I acknowledge the ﬁeld as involv- ing a degree of art, where problem formulation plays a major role in the outcome of a project. (This goes beyond ‘‘biasing’’ the search.) You seem to sidestep this aspect of problem formulation and focus largely on the paradigms, speciﬁcally, their representations and algorithms. But shouldn’t the Master Algorithm, ﬁrst and foremost, help converge on a good problem representation? A long-standing position in AI has been that if formulation is done ‘‘well,’’ the choice of which representation to use becomes quite obvi- ous. How would you respond? Dr. Domingos: Yes, perhaps the biggest difference be- tween the Master Algorithm and current learning algo- rithms is that the Master Algorithm can discover its own representations, and indeed entertain multiple representations at once, which is what makes humans so smart. This is why the Master Algorithm doesn’t just input data: it also inputs explicitly stated prior knowledge, whether previously discovered by it or obtained from humans. It can then reason with this knowledge and the data to form new generalizations. The knowledge is modular, composable, and declara- tive, so it can be reused. Again, this is in sharp contrast to what happens today, where there’s no reuse and learning is not cumulative. I think deep learning and reinforcement learning have made some progress toward discovering repre- sentations, but it only goes a small fraction of the way we need to go. The Master Algorithm can reason about alternate representations—it’s not just a ‘‘pure’’ learning algorithm, it also has the capabilities of clas- sic symbolic AI. And it can interact explicitly with the user to converge on a solution. This is not just a the- oretical idea; it’s what Markov logic networks do, and what Alchemy and other implementations of them enable. BIG: Since we’re on the subject of deep learning and at the risk of going off on a little tangent, is the recent success of deep learning on problems of perception aided by the fact that the data they consider—visual and auditory, for example—comes packaged with a lot of additional bonus information embedded within it? Pixels, for example, have information color, which comes from a predeﬁned range of values that carry in- formation about where they lie on a spectrum and so on, as well as ‘‘ordering’’ information in that you treat pixels in close physical proximity differently from if they are far away. This natural richness of informa- tion in the raw data doesn’t typically exist in other types of data such as business transactions where a lot of handcrafting is required to turn the raw data into a useful representation from which we can learn. Do you agree? Dr. Domingos: Pixels have spatial structure, and that helps. Sequential structure (e.g., time) also helps. But I think other domains besides perception often have structure as well (spatiotemporal, hierarchical, rela- tional, etc.), and exploiting it is deﬁnitely a very good starting point for machine learning. Deep learning does it, but there are other methods that do (e.g., statis- tical relational learning). BIG: I liked your analysis of the No Free Lunch Theorem, namely, that without knowledge there is no learning. The ﬂip side to this is that we care about reality more than we do about hypothetical worlds in which the learner will fail, and connecting INTERVIEW WITH PEDRO DOMINGOS 11

this to ‘‘bias’’ in Machine Learning. The NFLT might also be related to my question on formula- tion. Perhaps you get an almost free lunch if you’re clever about formulation, otherwise you pay. What do you think? Dr. Domingos: Formulation is only half the battle. Certainly, how you set up the problem as a machine learning one and the features you construct can make a big difference. But after all that is done, the NFLT still applies: all models are equally good a priori, and you need to incorporate further domain knowledge be- fore you can do better than random guessing. All learn- ing algorithms do this, to some extent (e.g., they make assumptions about similarity, continuity, indepen- dence, etc.), but in a limited and often implicit way. Which is why we need learners that can explicitly in- corporate a wide variety of knowledge, from very little to a lot. BIG: Let’s come back to some big picture issues. You make an intriguing argument at the outset of your book that ﬁelds of science with more data advance faster than those with less. You contrast molecular biology with neuroscience. Are there other compari- sons that would convince us that your proposed pat- tern isn’t overﬁtted?! Dr. Domingos: It’s not just whether ﬁelds have more data, it’s how much data they have relative to the com- plexity of the phenomena they study. For example, physics was the ﬁrst science to take off because it stud- ies the simplest phenomena, and even small amounts of data sufﬁce to get pretty far. Conversely, social sci- ence is tough because the phenomena are extremely complex, and until recently there was little data—but that’s changing. BIG: Talking about data in the social sciences, we seem to be in a situation where private companies such as Google and Facebook have most of the inter- esting data and the rest of us have very little. Not just that, they’re hiring all the best scientists from universities to work on their data. I joke with my friends in sociology that this is the golden age of the ﬁeld, since they can now observe human behav- ior at a scale and granularity not previously possi- ble. This is true in theory, they counter, but they can’t get the data! At a recent symposium at NYU on the ‘‘Future of AI,’’ Eric Schmidt made a point of saying that Google wants AI to beneﬁt the many and not the few. That’s commendable, and you seem equally optimistic about better societies and world peace due to ML. At the same time, I think you say somewhere that ‘‘he who controls the data controls the learner.’’ Will social good trump responsibility to shareholders? A skeptic might ask why we should expect the major data players to share data that advances science at the risk of diminishing their competitive advantage. The same skeptic might concede that these players will provide ‘‘standard data sets’’ that scientists can compete on and advance science and then be absorbed by them! What do you think? Dr. Domingos: I think that for businesses, business comes ﬁrst. So there are certainly limits to what they will do. The real answer is elsewhere: citizens need to become more aware of the value of data and of their re- sponsibility to share it for the common good, and we need the platforms, etcetera, that will make it easy. There’s a movement afoot to do this in cancer medi- cine, for example—sharing data from all patients and hospitals to learn predictive models for treatment, and so on—and hopefully it will succeed there and then expand to other areas. BIG: Lastly, you say early on that ‘‘Non-Machine Learning-oriented companies can’t compete with those using it.’’ This is an interesting question. Companies differ in terms of the inherent value of their data—many companies just don’t have the right data to do anything useful with it, machine learning or not, while others are naturally endowed with rich data. Some of this can depend on your place in the value chain in that industry. For exam- ple, an insurance company that sells in the B2B space and sells through agents has very different data from those that sell direct and have rich data about their customers or sales process. Is Machine Learning more important to some companies and relatively unimportant to others based on the inher- ent richness of their data? Dr. Domingos: I think that pretty much every company can do better by using data and machine learning. Com- panies that don’t have a lot of data have a problem— they need to start collecting it ASAP, either directly 12 INTERVIEW WITH PEDRO DOMINGOS

from the customer or by acquiring it from third parties, or they’ll be at a serious disadvantage compared with the ones that do. This doesn’t just mean relative to their direct competitors: companies that don’t have data won’t know how best to design and market their products, and as a result, those products risk be- coming commoditized, with most of the value being captured by the companies closer to the customer that do have that data. And ‘‘customer’’ doesn’t just mean consumer—it’s whoever buys your products and services, including other companies. Customers aside, machine learning can also be used extensively to optimize a company’s internal operations, and this is indeed becoming the norm. BIG: Thanks Pedro, and again, congratulations on a most excellent book. Cite this article as: Dhar V, Domingos P (2016) Pedro Domingos on The Master Algorithm: A conversation with Vasant Dhar.
